title: Issuance of Orders under Internal Security Act (ISA) against two self-radicalised Singaporean youths, and updates on ISA Orders

reading.body:
This is a case of online radicalisation producing offline attack planning, handled through an administrative detention regime rather than a criminal prosecution. The 17-year-old's plan to attack five mosques was formed and developed in an online environment, and the reporting attributes his radicalisation to far-right material encountered there. The 15-year-old's case follows the same pattern in the opposite direction, with allegiance pledged online and travel to Syria sought through flight searches. Both are cases where the intent was expressed and the preparation was underway, and where the physical capability to carry it out was the limiting factor.

The failure mode here is not a system error but a detection gap. Neither youth was stopped by a platform, a monitoring tool or an automated flag described in the reporting. The 17-year-old was an online contact of a person already detained, which means a link existed in data the authorities held, but the reporting does not say whether that link was used to find him or whether he was identified independently. What would have caught it earlier is not established by the facts given.

What is not established is how either youth was first identified, whether any platform reported them, or what specific evidence supported the orders. The restriction order and the detention are actions taken by the Internal Security Department, not findings by a court, and the reporting does not describe any judicial proceeding. The minister's remarks on rehabilitation are a statement of policy, not an assessment of either individual.

reports.title: Singaporean Islamic State supporter the first female youth caught under ISA; another teen detained for far-right extremism
Issuance of Orders under Internal Security Act (ISA) against two self-radicalised Singaporean youths, and updates on ISA Orders

summary:
Singapore's Internal Security Department said a 15-year-old girl became the first female youth and second-youngest person dealt with under the Internal Security Act. She supported the Islamic State, pledged allegiance to the group online, tried to find flights to Syria, and hoped to marry a fighter. She received a restriction order. A 17-year-old boy was detained after being radicalised by far-right material, identifying as an East Asian supremacist and planning attacks on five mosques, aiming to kill at least 100 people, though he could not get a gun.

The 17-year-old was an online contact of Nick Lee Xing Qiu, who was detained in December, but they did not know each other's plans. Since 2015, 17 youths aged 20 and below have been dealt with under the ISA. Minister K Shanmugam said families should alert the authorities if they suspect radicalisation, and noted many cases can be rehabilitated.
